'''John Gordon King''' (1925–2014<ref>{{Cite news|url = https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/obituaries/2014/07/05/john-king-cambridge-mit-physics-professor-directed-molecular-beam-lab-promoted-science-education/16QQu5B4eztIvpuDeVzamO/story.html|title = John G. King, 88; MIT professor|last = Marquard|first = Bryan|date = July 6, 2014|work = Boston Globe|accessdate = July 6, 2014}}</ref>) was an English-born American physicist who was the Francis Friedman Professor of Physics (emeritus) at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]],<ref>{{cite web|title=People Directory|url=http://web.mit.edu/bin/cgicso?query=alias%3DJ-king|publisher=MIT|accessdate=15 July 2011}}</ref> the former director of MIT’s Molecular Beam Laboratory,<ref name=honor>{{cite web|last=Bogatin|first=Eric|title=Professor King Honored by Students, Peers|date=12 April 2000 |url=http://web.mit.edu/newsoffice/2000/king-0412.html|publisher=MITnews|accessdate=15 July 2011}}</ref> and the former associate director of MIT’s [[Research Laboratory of Electronics]].<ref name="Research lab">{{cite web|title=MIT research lab|url=http://www.rle.mit.edu/|work=MIT}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=People|url=http://webmuseum.mit.edu/detail.php?t=people&type=browse&f=date1&s=1950&record=32|work=King, John G.|publisher=MIT Museum Collections|accessdate=20 September 2011}}</ref>

==Career==
Best known for his work on [[null hypothesis|null experiments]],<ref>{{cite journal|last=Bogatin|first=Eric|title=King of the Null Experiment is Honored|journal=Technology Review|date=June 2000}}</ref> King was also involved in the [[Physical Sciences Study Committee]] (PSSC)<ref>{{cite web|last=King|first=John G.|title=Personal Views of the Beginnings of PSSC and My Film Experiences|url=http://www.compadre.org/portal/pssc/docs/King.pdf|publisher=Physical Sciences Study Committee|accessdate=15 July 2011}}</ref><ref name=teach>{{cite web|last=Heiney|first=Paul A.|title=Movie List|url=https://www.physics.upenn.edu/demolab/movie.html|publisher=University of Pennsylvania Department of Physics and Astronomy|access-date=15 July 2011}}</ref>  with his doctoral advisor [[Jerrold Zacharias]]. Additionally, he is the inventor of the molecular [[microscope]].<ref>{{cite patent|country = US| number = 3790793| status = Patent| title = Molecular Scanner| gdate = 2/5/1974 | fdate = 11/5/1971| invent1 = John G. King| assign1 = MIT}}</ref>  He has received the Alfred P. Sloan Award (1956), the [[American Association of Physics Teachers]] (AAPT) Apparatus Competition prize (1961), the AAPT [[Robert A. Millikan award|Robert Millikan Medal]] (1965), the [[Danforth Foundation| Danforth Foundation's]] [[E. Harris Harbison]] Award for Gifted Teaching (1971), and most recently the [[Oersted Medal]] from the  AAPT in 2000.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.aapt.org/Programs/awards/millikan.cfm | title=Robert A. Millikan Medal}}</ref><ref name=awardO>{{cite journal|last=O'Kuma|first=Thomas|title=American Association of Physics Teachers 2000 Oersted Medalist: John G. King|journal=American Journal of Physics|date=January 2001|volume=69|issue=1|pages=10|url=http://link.aip.org/link/?AJPIAS/69/10/1|bibcode=2001AmJPh..69...10O|doi=10.1119/1.1320437|access-date=2019-05-18|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130925043901/http://link.aip.org/link/?AJPIAS/69/10/1|archive-date=2013-09-25|url-status=dead|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Oersted Medal|url=http://www.aapt.org/Programs/awards/oersted.cfm|publisher=American Association of Physics Teachers|accessdate=15 July 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=John G King|url=http://academictree.org/physics/peopleinfo.php?pid=4177|accessdate=15 July 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Oerstaed and Richtmeyer Memorial Lecture|url=http://scitation.aip.org/getpdf/servlet/GetPDFServlet?filetype=pdf&id=PHTEAH000038000004000203000001&idtype=cvips&prog=normal|publisher=AAPT Awards|accessdate=15 July 2011}}</ref>

King obtained undergraduate (1950) and graduate degrees (1953) in physics from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and soon after he was appointed to the faculty there.<ref name=awardO/> As a young professor, he helped produce and acted in several PSSC educational movies, including Time and Clocks, Interference of Photons, Size of Atoms from an Atomic Beam Experiment, and Velocity of Atoms.<ref name=teach/>  King also developed innovative courses such as Concentrated Study, Project Lab,<ref>{{cite journal|last=King|first=John|title=On Physics Project Laboratories|journal=Robert A. Millikan Lecture|date=26 May 1966|volume=2|url=http://scitation.aip.org/getpdf/servlet/GetPDFServlet?filetype=pdf&id=AJPIAS000034000011001058000001&idtype=cvips&prog=normal|accessdate=19 September 2011}}</ref> and Corridor Lab,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://web.mit.edu/Edgerton/www/CorridorLab.html|work=Edgerton Center|publisher=MIT|title=Corridor Lab|date=June 2023 }}</ref> which emphasized hands-on learning, independence of thought, and the scientific method.<ref name=honor /><ref>{{cite web|last=French|first=Anthony P.|title=Physics Education at MIT: From Bell's Phonautograph to Technology Enhanced Active Learning|url=http://web.mit.edu/physics/news/physicsatmit/physicsatmit_05_french.pdf|accessdate=15 July 2011}}</ref>

King’s null experiments included searching for [[Electric charge|charge]] equality between the [[proton]] and [[electron]], [[quark]]s, [[magnetic monopole]]s, and a variant of the  [[Steady State theory|continuous creation theory]] of matter proposed by [[Fred Hoyle]], [[Thomas Gold]], and [[Hermann Bondi]].
